passages.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Fact Sheet & Patient Education
passages.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition that affects women of reproductive age, with an estimated prevalence of 8% to 13% worldwide. It is characterized by hormonal imbalances, irregular or absent ovulation, higher-than-normal levels of androgens (male-type hormones), and small fluid-filled follicles (sac-like structures) in the ovaries. Irregular periods alone do not confirm PCOS; clinical assessment by a healthcare professional is required.

passages.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Fact Sheet & Patient Education
passages.text: Symptoms of PCOS vary from person to person and may change over time. Common symptoms include heavy, long, intermittent, unpredictable, or absent menstrual periods (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea); excess facial or body hair (hirsutism); persistent acne or oily skin; scalp hair thinning or male-pattern baldness; weight gain especially around the abdomen; difficulty conceiving (infertility due to irregular ovulation); and darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans) associated with insulin resistance.

passages.title: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome 2023
passages.text: While the genetic predisposition to PCOS cannot be prevented, healthy lifestyle management is recommended for all individuals with PCOS to improve metabolic, reproductive, and psychological health and reduce long-term risks such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Evidence-based habits include regular physical activity (at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening exercises twice weekly), a balanced nutrient-dense diet rich in fiber, whole grains, lean proteins, fruits, and vegetables, adequate sleep hygiene, and stress reduction. No single specific diet outperforms a balanced healthy eating pattern.

passages.title: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome 2023
passages.text: In adults (18 years and older), clinical evaluation for PCOS typically uses the revised Rotterdam criteria, which require at least two of the following three features after excluding other conditions (such as thyroid disorders or hyperprolactinemia): (1) irregular or absent ovulatory cycles, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or elevated anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels as assessed by a clinician.

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.locator: Section 1: What is Menstruation & Normal Cycle Range
passages.text: Menstruation is the normal monthly shedding of the uterine lining (endometrium) driven by cyclical changes in reproductive hormones (estrogen, progesterone, LH, and FSH). In adults, a typical menstrual cycle ranges from 21 to 35 days, with menstrual bleeding lasting between 2 and 7 days. Menstrual irregularities include cycles shorter than 21 days (polymenorrhea), longer than 35 days (oligomenorrhea), absent periods for 3 or more months (amenorrhea), or abnormally heavy bleeding (menorrhagia).

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.locator: Section 2: Menstrual Symptoms & When Cycles Change
passages.text: Common menstrual symptoms include mild-to-moderate lower abdominal or pelvic cramping (primary dysmenorrhea caused by uterine prostaglandins), lower back ache, breast tenderness, bloating, headache, fatigue, and premenstrual mood changes. Symptoms that interfere with daily activities, sudden changes in cycle regularity, bleeding between periods, or soaking through one or more pads or tampons every hour for two consecutive hours warrant medical evaluation.

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.text: General lifestyle habits that support healthy menstrual function and help reduce mild menstrual discomfort include regular aerobic physical activity, applying a warm heating pad or taking a warm bath to relax uterine muscles, staying well hydrated, consuming iron-rich foods (such as leafy greens, legumes, and lean meats) paired with vitamin C to prevent iron deficiency from menstrual blood loss, maintaining consistent sleep, managing stress, avoiding smoking, and practicing safe menstrual hygiene by changing menstrual products regularly.

passages.title: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle: Overview, Irregularities, and Self-Care
passages.text: Seek immediate emergency medical care if menstrual or pelvic symptoms are accompanied by: soaking through 1 or more sanitary pads or tampons every hour for 2+ consecutive hours; severe, sudden, or worsening lower abdominal or pelvic pain; dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting (syncope), or shortness of breath; possible pregnancy combined with vaginal bleeding or one-sided pelvic/shoulder pain (to rule out ectopic pregnancy); or high fever and chills with pelvic pain or foul-smelling discharge.
